description: I'm a Computer Science graduate from Ethiopia, a science communicator, and a passionate space enthusiast. I enjoy exploring technology, astronomy, and innovative solutions to real-world challenges. I believe great ideas come from collaboration and different perspectives.
summary:
Team Andromeda Aerospace presents Lunar Site Explorer, an intuitive 3D web application designed to accelerate lunar mission planning. The Moon's South Pole presents extreme lighting and communication constraints, making rapid site evaluation critical when launch schedules shift. Unlike complex traditional tools, our solution allows users to visually drop pins anywhere on an interactive, high-resolution 3D Moon to instantly assess local conditions.

The app calculates precise Sun and Earth elevations and azimuths, displaying 48-hour operational timelines and allowing users to compare multiple sites and dates side-by-side. To ensure scientific accuracy, we integrated the NASA JPL Horizons API to validate our browser-based orbital calculations against official ephemerides, alongside high-resolution LRO imagery from NASA Moon Trek.

By transforming raw astronomical data into clear, interactive visualizations, Lunar Site Explorer bridges the gap between complex science and agile engineering, empowering mission planners, educators, and the public to make faster, data-driven decisions for Artemis and future lunar missions
details:
How does it work?
Lunar Site Explorer is an interactive 3D web application that transforms complex lunar ephemeris data into intuitive visualizations. Users can click anywhere on a high-resolution 3D globe of the Moon, or select from a curated list of historical and future landing sites (like Apollo 11 or Shackleton Crater). Upon selecting a site, the app instantly calculates the local horizon and plots the current positions of the Sun and Earth. It features a 2D polar sky plot, a 48-hour timeline graph showing operational windows, and a date-picker "time machine" to simulate how conditions change over time.

What benefits does it have?
The primary benefit is speed and clarity for rapid scenario comparison. If a mission launch is delayed, planners can change the date in our app and instantly see how the new power generation and communication windows are affected. It replaces the tedious process of cross-referencing raw data tables with instant visual feedback. Additionally, dynamic 3D lighting reflects the actual Sun position, and multi-site comparison allows users to evaluate different locations side-by-side.

What is the intended impact?
Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex scientific data and agile mission planning. By making the extreme environmental constraints of the lunar South Pole visually obvious, the tool helps mission planners de-risk Artemis and CLPS missions. Furthermore, it serves as an accessible educational tool for the public and students, requiring no PhD to understand why small changes in location or date have massive impacts on mission feasibility.

Tools, Languages, and Software Used:

  • Languages: Vanilla JavaScript (ES6), HTML5, CSS3.
  • Libraries & Frameworks: Three.js (for WebGL 3D rendering), astronomy-engine (for local VSOP87/ELP2000 orbital mathematics), and HTML5 Canvas (for custom chart generation). We used Vite as our build tool to bundle the application.
  • NASA APIs: We integrated the JPL Horizons API for real-time ephemeris validation and the NASA Moon Trek WMTS API to fetch high-resolution LRO imagery of specific landing sites.
  • Architecture: 100% client-side. No backend servers were used, ensuring zero latency and high scalability.

How is your project creative?
We took a "visual-first" approach to a highly mathematical problem. Instead of presenting dry data tables, we built a "Google Earth-style" interface for the Moon. Our creativity shines in features like the Dynamic 3D Shadowing, where the actual 3D lighting on the Moon changes based on the calculated Sun position, and our Mission Context Cards, which dynamically display geographical and historical mission information (such as CSA Artemis contributions at the South Pole) based on the coordinates clicked.

Factors the Team Considered:

  • Scientific Accuracy: We prioritized mathematical integrity. We wrote custom coordinate transformation logic (astro.js) to convert Earth-centric vectors into the Moon's selenographic local horizon frame, and built a validation tool to prove our math matches NASA JPL Horizons within a fraction of a degree.
  • Performance: By keeping the app 100% client-side and avoiding heavy frontend frameworks like React, we guaranteed lightning-fast performance.
  • Topography: We considered the extreme terrain of the lunar South Pole. While our MVP uses a smooth sphere for instant calculations, we designed the architecture to eventually ingest LOLA DEM (Digital Elevation Model) data to calculate precise terrain horizon masking.
